utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, will you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you Mr. President. Case number IT-01-47-T, the Prosecutor versus Enver Hadzihasanovic and Amir Kubura.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Can we have the appearances for the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours, counsel, and everyone in and around the courtroom. For the Prosecution, Stefan Waespi, Mathias Neuner, and Daryl Mundis, assisted by our case manager, Andres Vatter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Mundis. The appearances for the Defence now, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. On behalf of General Enver Hadzihasanovic, Edina Residovic, counsel; Stephane Bourgon, co-counsel; and Alexis Demirdjian, legal assistant. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The other Defence team, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. On behalf of Mr. Kubura, Rodney Dixon, Fahrudin Ibrisimovic, and Nermin Mulalic, legal assistant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Chamber on Tuesday, the 15th of February, 2005 bids good morning to all those present, the representatives of the Prosecution, all the attorneys, the two accused, as well as the witness, who is present in the courtroom. And I do not wish to omit mention of the personnel of this courtroom as well as those outside the courtroom. We need to continue the testimony of this witness within the framework of the cross-examination, and I shall give the floor now to Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Veseljak.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I'd like to continue our discussion about a few of the exhibits, and the first one I want to talk about is -- comes out of the bundle of the Defence. So if you could also be given the binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, the document I want to talk about is one of the judgements, and that's part of the fourth tab, the fourth big tab, and it's the second document within the fourth tab, subtitled "Judgement." And specifically that's Defence Exhibit DH155/7, and it's a judgement of 3rd June 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Did you find that, Mr. Veseljak?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, here -- you weren't the -- one of the judges, I see, but the presiding judge was a Mr. Strika. And first of all, that's again one of these crimes you mentioned yesterday. You see it both in the English and B/C/S version, the bottom of page 2 and 3. The issue is the willful abandonment of positions, stealing of cows, stealing of children's bicycles, and so on. That's basically what this judgement is about. I'm interested in though -- in page 6, the second paragraph in your language, B/C/S. Page 6, second paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And in English, Your Honours, it's the last paragraph on page 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And I'll read it out for the benefit of -- of everybody: "During the presentation of evidence at trial, with the parties' consent, the court read the records of witness interviews held with witnesses Mirsad Ehic, perhaps, and Avdo Buljubasic from preliminary proceedings, examined the report by the battalion of the 303rd Mountain Brigade, a document certifying that the accused were members of the 303rd Zenica Mountain Brigade, a certificate for the temporarily confiscated items, and a copy of the criminal records of the accused." Now, Mr. Veseljak, what I would like you to help us is this mentioning of a document certifying that the accused were members of the 303rd Zenica Mountain Brigade. Now, what are these certificates? Who issues them, if you know?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are certificates or a document which in principle was issued by the brigade indicating the name of the brigade and the text that such-and-such a person was a member of that brigade, and it was on that basis that the competence was established -- or rather, the capacity of the person as a military person. So such certificates or receipts could in principle be issued by a civilian body responsible for mobilisation. In most cases we had certificates issued by brigades indicating that a certain person was a member of such an entity at a certain point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And the court authorities, the judges, they would rely on this information.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As these are documents as a public document, then the assumption is that they are correct. Should that be questioned, then it could be verified.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's move on to a second issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, I have another document I would like to show the witness which is not contained in the bundle I have -- you have been given yesterday. That's P660, Exhibit P660. It's -- it's a short document, just -- just one page. It appears to be a document dated 1st April from the 306rd Mountain Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, what I'm interested in, Mr. Veseljak, and perhaps you can help us after you have familiarised yourself briefly with its contents, what I'm mostly interested in is item 3, "Unusual incidents and relations with the HVO," just at the bottom of it. And let me read out again what I have in the English version: "In the afternoon of 31st March 1993, the body of a foreign citizen in a BH army uniform was found by the Zabilje village, Zukica-Most road. The investigating judge took on the case and the security organ will send details of this," and then it goes on to talk about the impact it had on the HVO. Now, it talks about a investigating military judge who took on the case. Do you remember this incident? Is it possible that you were concerned with this incident?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think one of the Defence counsel has something to raise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Our remark has -- relates to the fact that this document obviously relates to the Travnik military court, so it doesn't apply to the region of Zenica municipality nor the district military court of Zenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecution, you asked the witness whether he was involved in this case, and the Defence tells us that this area is within the jurisdiction of the Travnik military court and not of the one to which the witness belonged.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, I believe the witness testified yesterday about the jurisdiction of the Zenica high court, and he said there were two military courts - the one in Zenica and then the one in Travnik - and I think five or six other military courts or basic courts. He didn't say in which area he was exercising his jurisdiction as a duty judge. At least, I'm not aware. And he can certainly tell us whether, you know, he was involved in that incident or not. That's entirely up to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ask him whether he was competent to investigate in the zone of the village of Zabilje.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: You heard the question of the Presiding Judge. Were you competent to investigate an incident which occurred in this Zabilje village, Zukica-Most area or road?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I explained -- the Prosecutor probably misunderstood. In this area we were talking about, there were two district military courts and five or six basic civilian courts, not military courts. So the court I worked in did not have territorial jurisdiction over this location that is referred to in this document, so I'm not familiar with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, in your area, were you ever called to attend the scene where a foreign citizen was found in an ABiH uniform? Did that ever occur to you?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never. It never happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you. If the document could be returned.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: The next issue I would like to raise with you involves three exhibits in your bundle, the bundle I gave you, yes, to the left. And these are tabs 11, 12, and 13. And it involves Exhibits P777 - that's tab 11 - Exhibit P779 - that's tab 12 - and Exhibit P774 - that's tab 13. Now, this appears to involve a incident, if we start with tab 11, that occurred in May, early May. And if you look at first Exhibit 11 -- at tab 11; that's Exhibit P777. That's an order from the Operations Group Lasva, the command, and the order was given to the commander obviously of the 309th Brigade. Now, this order says that something has happened, an unfortunate incident, and the order is to this commander of the 309th Brigade that he immediately look into it and issue a written report. That's under item 1. And item 2 - I'm still tab 11 of that order dated 5th May, 1993 - it says what exactly he needs to do, meaning taking written statements of people such as Chief of Staff, commander of companies, and so on, and he's been given a couple of days to complete this order. Can you see that in this document?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, the second document is just a few days later. That's tab 12; Prosecution Exhibit 779. And here obviously the commander of the 309th Brigade has completed what he has been ordered. He talks about the Chetnik ambush on the first page, and he lists on the last page, page 4, in the English version, he lists his report as an attachment and also the statements of various people, as ordered. Now, the document I would like to ask you is now the last document. This is tab 13. That's a criminal report dated 31st of July, 1993. It appears to originate from the 3rd Corps command and is signed by a Mr. Dugalic, as it appears on this page. That's P Exhibit 774, addressed to the military prosecutor's office in Zenica. Now, what you can see here is that apparently the 3rd Corps has looked into this issue and he basically directs the military prosecutor's office to take measures to identify the individual who perpetrated this crime as well as possibly other crimes and to instigate criminal proceedings against him before the military court in Zenica which has jurisdiction in the matter. It also in the last paragraph, the last sentence says: "By interrogating of witnesses on all of the circumstances surrounding the crime." And then the annexes list the report we have seen in the previous document and statements. Now, my question to you is: Is that the typical course of action that the military look first into their side and then they hand the -- their findings, their witness statements, over to the military prosecutor with certain directions or guidelines? Would that be a normal course of action, Mr. Veseljak?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Except for the fact that I wish to point out at the beginning nobody gave instructions or orders to the prosecutor's office, and that applies to this case too. I'm afraid you're misinterpreting this document. The prosecutor's office is given a proposal to act in that way. The criminal report contains a description of the event and the proposal of the author of the criminal report to the prosecutor's office to institute criminal proceedings. We have here two completely different aspects of an event. It was customary in all cases to first investigate whether there was any reason to file a criminal report against someone and only then to actually file it, and it is normal to expect, and what happened in practice was that in addition to a criminal report, attention was drawn to the existence of evidence which leads to suspect that there are grounds for prosecution. And once that suspicion is established, then the prosecution is instigated on the basis of well-founded suspicions. So the direct answer to your question would be that in this document, I do not see anything out of the ordinary. The military unit along its chain of command carries out internal checks in accordance with the rules of service, and if there is a suspicion that someone has committed a criminal offence and once that is established, it is forwarded to the prosecutor. The law provided for the obligation of every citizen and every institution to inform the prosecutor of any possible commission of a criminal offence, and that is what happened here.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. That's -- that's your answer. Thank you very much on this aspect. Let me move on to a next point. You told us that you were involved, I think, in a case, an investigating judgement, I don't recall about, of an Egyptian citizen who is I think now a doctor in -- in Egypt. Do you remember that, talking about that yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember. This event I was involved in, that is, in the proceedings, I mentioned it only as an illustration of the various difficulties we encountered, including difficulties in identifying people, and it was part of my answer to a question from the Defence as to the difficulties we had to grapple with. As far as I can remember, this event occurred much later in relation to the period covered by these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, if we could briefly go into private session for -- for a couple of minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are in open session, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the re-examination, the Defence has the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Veseljak.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, Colleague Residovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday my learned friend from the Prosecution asked you several questions showing you records of on-site inspections that you may have attended or one of your colleagues, judges, from the district military court. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In this connection, he also asked you a large number of questions that you answered which was -- were intended to show that it was important for the judge to know the name of the suspect, to establish certain facts, to seize weapons, to collect the names of witnesses, and so on. Do you remember that that was the gist of the questions put to you by the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In connection with this whole set of questions put to you while you were shown certain documents, my question to you is whether these were relevant facts which the judge when he goes to the crime scene seeks to establish.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we are talking about an on-site investigation, we are never establishing facts. We are just collecting what is to be found on site and any possible information that one may gather on site. I would be prone to say in the Croatian version an "Uvidjaj" is called an "Ocevid," a different word is used meaning that one notes down what one sees with one's eyes. But the judge carrying out the on-site inspection will seek to collect as much information as he can which may be of use to him later on.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Answering a question from my learned friend - and I don't wish to quote from the transcript - you said on a number of occasions -- you used the phrase "if possible." Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please: When you tell us "collecting all possible facts which may be of importance for the case," is this limited by the possibilities of the time and space and all other constraints that a judge may have when he goes on site?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. Every on-site investigation is limited by the situation under which it is carried out. I can give you ten main questions that need to be answered if we were to act in accordance with theory. But every on-site investigation was limited by circumstances, and that is why sometimes most detailed information was collected and at other times only very rough information. And a third possibility would be when you arrived and found absolutely nothing. Then you did not carry out an on-site investigation; you just filed an official note saying that you didn't find anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Veseljak, when a judge goes on site, who determines whether it is possible to carry out certain steps or not?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The judge.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When the judge goes to the crime scene, who determines which facts will be collected and in which way? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, the judge.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When the judge is at the scene, a military body, the military police, or the civilian police or anyone else, can they take over this role from the judge and determine what can be established and which facts need to be collected?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No one speaks at an on-site investigation except the judge, so no one can make any decision, a positive, a negative one, a wise or a stupid one, except the investigating judge.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In a number of on-site investigation reports shown to you, most of which you attended in person, one can see that either an autopsy was carried out or a description of the injuries suffered by a certain person. Who decides what the pathologist will do in each particular case?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The investigating judge.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In virtually all the documents shown to you, the name of the doctor pathologist appears. Do you know his name?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Faruk Turkic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Veseljak, in view of the fact that you were a judge throughout the war and you carried out on-site investigations, how much faith did you have in the description of injuries provided by Dr. Turkic and his post-mortem reports?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolute confidence. Dr. Turkic due to circumstances was for many years and the only pathologist in the cantonal hospital in Zenica. He's a person with a great deal of experience and a man of exceptional moral qualities. And my relationship goes back many years and I don't know of a single case, and Mr. Turkic is not a forensic pathologist, and in some cases when he is not authorised, we did engage forensic specialists like Professor Zdenko Cihlas, who is head of the chair of forensic medicine at the university to provide his report, but they never clashed with the findings of Dr. Turkic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: My learned friend as well as myself showed you a report on an investigation at Stranjani, where members of a military police battalion clashed with thieves. In answer to a question from my learned friend, you said - and I'm paraphrasing - that this was not the cow that was at stake. You explained that this was a checkpoint manned by members of the military police. Who were those military policemen protecting on the road?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: At this particular checkpoint, they were protecting the inhabitants of the village of Stranjani and the hinterland, because this is an area mostly inhabited by Croats. So the purpose of that checkpoint was to protect the population there and all of us, I have to add, who in one way or another were involved, either in handing out justice or protecting people, had a very strong feeling of need to protect that population. I can illustrate this: That when I went to carry out the investigation into that event, I asked a highly respectable man called Mr. Stipan, as we all called him, a Franciscan priest, to come with me to assist in dispelling the fear of those people and showing them that there is a legal entity taking care of their security, and hence this particular case is one that I certainly and definitely do not see as an event prompted by a -- the killing of a cow. The intention was to protect the people in their homes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My learned friend showed you today several documents linked to investigations into an event which occurred within the Operative Group Lasva. And in that connection, I would like to ask you the following: If a military unit, the military police, or the civilian police learns of an event the indicia of which point to grounds to suspect that there was a criminal offence, you explained that they themselves collect certain evidence before addressing the competent prosecutor's office. Is that what you were explaining in answer to a question from the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Because otherwise, if the prosecutor received a piece of paper saying, "I'm reporting such-and-such a person," then every normal reasonable prosecutor would ask him, "How would I know that that person is suspect?" Also, every citizen was duty-bound to inform the prosecutor that he has certain information that a crime had been committed. Such an individual is not expected to produce any documents in favour of such an assertion but all other bodies are.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Exhibit P777 and P779 and P774, you can have another look at them, please. They related to the death of certain soldiers in a military unit during a combat operation. Is that a fair description of the consideration given to this event by the army itself?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is my understanding, though I read it through in haste. There was a military operation. Certain people were killed. And then within the command structure, verifications were made as to whether any military rules were violated. A conclusion was reached that there were. And then there was, I think, a report against the armed forces. Under number 13 I think it is. I think I read it correctly, that -- that the criminal act of failing to secure a military unit. It belongs to the chapter of offences against the armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: My question to you, Mr. Veseljak, is: If you look at these records and reports and a criminal report against an unknown person, do these documents tell you the way in which the army investigated any acts of negligence on the part of their own soldiers or do you believe that this was an inappropriate way of investigating and disciplining one's own troops?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Every incident - and there were many - implied carrying out this kind of procedure, because the competent commander or command might discover that there were certain elements of disciplinary offences and a commander could have sentenced the person to 30 days of military detention or not allowing him any free time or maybe someone may have committed a misdemeanour and be reported to a magistrate court. But somebody here came to the conclusion that there were grounds to suspect that a criminal offence had been committed and this was reported to the district military prosecutor. Theoretically the following stage would be for the prosecutor to consider the matter, then to address it to the investigating judge in Travnik, to carry out an investigation, and then the procedure continues according to the rules.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Veseljak, we were at war, and there's -- it is quite obvious that people at war get killed. And if a military commander or the military police would find that somebody was killed in combat and if they found that there were no grounds to suspect anything else, would it be customary for the army to complete the investigation without any other judicial bodies being informed, or did it have to inform them?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Normal casualties in combat operations were dealt with within the military structure, without informing any judicial body. However, whenever there was any grounds to suspect, well-founded or unfounded grounds - there were many such cases - even if this happened on the front, then the duty judge would be informed and he would carry out the investigation. So the answer is if somebody was killed in combat, the judicial organs were not informed about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: If the military body, the police or someone else, felt that immediately after the event a judicial body had to be informed, first the duty judge and then the prosecutor, and if the duty judge goes on site, who after that determines the further course of proceedings?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And at the investigation itself?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The investigating judge.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can the military body that knows the judicial authorities have taken over the case, can they independently carry out any acts on their own contrary to instructions from the court?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I understand you well, let me say the following: No one can prohibit the commander from continuing to look into people's behaviour, conduct, from the standpoint of military discipline. However, regarding influence over criminal proceedings, that has absolutely no purpose. There are no parallel investigations or anything else that can affect the criminal proceedings. The moment the investigating judge is on site, the case is in the hands of the judiciary.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: One more question, Mr. Veseljak: You were shown a report dated the 19th of April, when Zenica was shelled. In a part of the instructions you gave, there was the instruction that the civil defence should clean up the area after the on-site investigation had been completed. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, does the civil defence have its own legally prescribed competencies, or do they have to wait for the investigating judge?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have taken a deep breath because whenever the 19th is mentioned, those horrific pictures come back. The civil defence acts in accordance with the law on civil defence. It has its own organisational structure and its chain of command and links between the court and the civil defence don't really exist. However, in this particular case, the highly -- the very limited resources of the city, including resources that could be used to wash the pavement, such as a water tank, were subordinated to the civil defence. And this terrible event took place in the centre of town in an area five times the size of this courtroom, where 15 people were killed and 49 people seriously injured. It is the spot where the largest department store is, the central mosque, and an old part of town full of cafes which were full of people. So this was a meeting place. This is the only place that was lit up during the war at night. And naturally, after this terrible tragedy, I thought it absolutely essential to ask the civil defence after the investigation to clean up this part of town because that was the only place where the citizens gathered and we couldn't leave it like that, and that is why I gave such orders. But the civil defence has a completely different function. It acts according to its own rules and duties.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Veseljak, do you know Mesic Mirsad? As you were an inhabitant of Zenica, what was he during the war?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do know him, but I must say as a layman he was head of the civil defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Wait a moment, please. There seems to be an objection from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, I don't -- I sort of gather what -- where the Defence is going right now, but I just ask in cross-examination one factual question to the witness, whether he ordered the civil protection people to clean it. And from this now the Defence talks about jurisdiction of the Municipal Defence Staff. It goes into other people mentioning. I think that goes way beyond the scope of redirect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ask your question slowly, going towards your objective, not through a single question which can be considered to be leading and which can go beyond the scope of the cross-examination. So according to my understanding, you want to ask him about the civil defence or protection. Is that right? Is civil defence the object of your interest?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. The Prosecutor, because he found it important to ask whether it is the court that ordered the civil defence to clean up this area in Zenica -- I'm not going into the way in which he will use his -- this answer in his arguments. I asked the witness the same question, and he explained that it was due to circumstances that he gave such an order but that the civil defence does its own work. And I just asked him whether he knows Mr. Mesic, a witness who testified in this court. He said he knew him and knows what his duties were. I have only one more question to this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: If Witness Mesic under oath would say in this court and said in this court that it is the legal obligation and duty of the civil defence to sanitise the area, that is, in areas of combat to collect bodies, to remove dead animals and clean up in other ways, do you consider that that witness is fully authorised to explain the competencies of the civil defence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before answering, the Defence wants to hear from the witness whether it is part of the duty of civil defence to clean up a combat area if there were casualties and dead people or dead animals. So it's a legal question. Is it up to the civil defence irrespective of any intervention by the judge to clean up the area? And she is saying that there is a witness who said that. And can the judge who is in front of us confirm that legally that is the obligation of the civil defence? So that is the question put to the witness. What is the objection of the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, again, we are in redirect. I asked a very simple question to the judge in connection with Zenica, the cleaning up. He gave a very good answer in redirect. Now, to go and ask him about another witness who testified here and who gave his opinion - and it may be right, it may be wrong; I don't know - is inappropriate at this point in redirect. And it's -- and it's also a leading question, at this point, by the way, to ask him or confirm or not what somebody else said. It's inappropriate at this point, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I shall try and bypass the difficulty asking the question myself, as it is a question of law, of interest to us Judges. To the best of your knowledge, did the civil defence have the legal obligation to clean up a combat area if in that area there were people killed or animals killed, irrespective of any intervention by a judge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They had such a legal obligation. And as far as I unfortunately know, that is what actually -- they actually did, as I had the misfortune of living through that war.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I have no more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The other Defence team?

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No additional questions. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] During the ten minutes before Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the break, I would like to ask you a few purely technical questions of a judicial nature but to inform the Judges, because I have to tell you at this point in time, regarding the rights of investigating judges or judges generally, there's a certain ambiguity in my mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to know -- I thought I had gathered on the basis of what you said that in this military court there's a judge that is on duty, and you said there were eight of you and you took turns. So you were on duty every eight weeks. Are you confirming that there was a duty judge over a certain period of time to deal with any problems that he may be informed of by the police, be it the civilian or the military police or anyone else?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Every week one of us was appointed as the duty judge by the Presiding Judge. This was done in a decision. And copies of the decision were forwarded and the civilian police and military police were informed of the appointment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Everyone can follow that. If there is an event -- let's imagine the following scenario: Somewhere a soldier who was killed is discovered. We don't know anything about the circumstances. There is a dead soldier and there are gunshot wounds. Does the civilian police or the military police then phone the judge and the person found in a public space is not in the battlefield. It's somewhere else. What happens in such a case?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At that point in time, the police first secure the site and inform the duty investigative judge. The duty investigative judge then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The French translation now said the "investigative judge." Let's be very clear. The judge, the duty judge, is it a judge or an investigative judge? Because in the documents that you signed, it says "judge"; however, there's another document in which it says "investigative judge." It's one of your colleagues. So is it an investigative judge or a judge that you are referring to? Because I believe that this is what is going to cause confusion. The duty judge, is it a judge or an investigative judge?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, allow me to provide you a somewhat lengthier explanation. Given the annual schedule that we had and in accordance with the rules for the procedure of the court, we were signed certain duties by the presiding judge. So I was assigned the duty as the presiding judge in first-instance cases. My colleague Ahmetovic was given the annual assignment of an investigative judge. However, when I was on duty -- when I'm on duty, I act as an investigative judge with authority that the investigative judge has according to the law. So I can order autopsies to be performed, exhumations to be performed, because these were actions for which only the investigative judge was responsible. So to answer your question, Mr. President, when I was on duty, I then acted as an investigative judge, as far as compiling documents are concerned. If you have a look at the heading at the introduction of my document, you will see that it always says that I worked as the duty investigative judge and that I was informed as the duty investigative judge of the cantonal court. But in fact I only signed the documents as "judge."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So the judge would go to the site where the body was found. The site was secured by the civilian or by the military police. You would then take a series of steps. That is what you said. And this is what could be seen in the document. You'd make a record, describe the body, the wounds that could be seen, the transport to the hospital, to the morgue, the autopsy, et cetera, et cetera. All this is referred to. And then you compile a report. This report, as far as I have understood you, is to be forwarded to the prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And I would usually also send a copy to the police assisting the on-site investigation because they also had a file that had to be complete and had to contain a copy of my record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So you would draft a report. But when reading all the documents of the Defence and the Prosecution, we can see that this is a very descriptive report. There aren't many personal assessments of the judge with regard to whether a crime was committed or not. But if a crime was committed, the prosecutor would have the report. And if I have understood you correctly, after this stage, if the prosecutor wanted to proceed and continue with the investigation, he had to make an official request and had to forward it to the investigative judge in order to initiate an investigation and to accuse someone who was suspected of being the perpetrator of the crime. Is this how things would actually take place?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then the investigative judge, who received the request, has the authority to interview witnesses, to interview the suspect or the accused, to order expert reports to be drafted, and to order any other useful investigations to be conducted. Can you confirm that this is actually how you would proceed?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Apart from the fact that the investigative judge would not express his own opinion. This was not the case according to our procedure. He could order expert reports to be drafted. He could interview anyone. But he would not express his opinion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When the investigative judge who received the request completed his work, he would then send his case file to the prosecutor. And having read the judgements, I believe that then the prosecutor drafts an indictment which is referred to the tribunal, to the court. Is that how things proceeded?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: If he was satisfied with the investigation conducted, if he believed that it wasn't necessary to continue with the investigation or widen its scope, then he would draft this indictment. Otherwise, the case would be annulled.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Were there situations in which the investigative judge would go to the site, make a record, send it to the prosecutor, and then the prosecutor would do nothing? He would just put the case file on the shelf. He wouldn't send a request to the investigative judge and he would shelve the case? Did such things happen?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's one decision that the prosecutor could take. When you say to place the case file in the archives, it doesn't mean he wouldn't do anything. He would examine the case, decide that there were no grounds for further [Realtime transcript read in error "on if"] proceedings. He would compile an official note. That's how it was done. He would file a note saying that there are no grounds to continue [as interpreted] with the proceedings, with the case, and that would be that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Yesterday you said on a number of occasions in response to Defence questions that the prosecutor always remained responsible, always had competencies. We can see how important the role of the prosecutor is. It is the prosecutor who decides about further action to be taken in the light of the record compiled by the duty judge. If the prosecutor believes that it is not necessary to continue with the investigation by forwarding a request to the investigative judge, in such a case he shelves the case. So he has such absolute power. The judge has nothing to say in the matter.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he has nothing to say, nor does the court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Because since the court wasn't seized of the affair, there's nothing for the court to say. Very well. It is now quarter to 11.00. We will now have a break and we will resume at ten past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will now resume. Yes, Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, just for the sake of the transcript, on page 40, line 21, it says "on if proceedings." I don't know what the "if" means, but it doesn't make the witness's answer understandable. Line 22 it says he would file a note to continue; whereas, the witness said that -- whereas, the witness said "not to continue," and the witness did not say "to continue." Could this just be corrected, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I have a few more technical questions for you. When the prosecutor decides not to send a request to the investigative judge because he believes that there are not -- there's not sufficient evidence to accuse someone of having committed an offence, in such a case can the victims contest the decision not to proceed and forward a request either to the court or to the prosecutor, a request for the decision to be changed, or is no one aware of this decision and the victim is in fact not informed? Could you provide us with some information about this.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Victims cannot complain, cannot contest the prosecutor's decision not to continue with the proceedings, whether -- with the investigations. But when the prosecutor decides not to continue with proceedings, it is his duty to inform the victims. And after -- within eight days from having received this decision, they can continue with the proceedings themselves. In such a case, the victims take on the role of the prosecutor and they have all the rights that the prosecutor has. They can then request further investigations and other measures in accordance with the law. They can't contest the decision, but they can take on the role of the prosecutor and continue with the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So you have told us about two matters: Firstly, the prosecutor has the duty to inform within eight days of his decision the victims, inform them of the fact that he has shelved the case. And in such a case, the victims, according to the law and the procedure in force, may take action and request an investigation. I assume that this is done through a lawyer. How does this actually take place?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, technically speaking, it's done through a lawyer, but it's not necessary for this to be done through a lawyer. I'd just like to correct something. It's not the prosecutor's duty to inform the injured party within eight days. He must inform the victims immediately and then the victim has eight days to decide whether or not to continue with the affair. The victim does this by sending a one-sentence letter to the prosecutor and saying, "In accordance with your report," such-and-such a number, such-and-such a date, "I hereby inform you that I wish to continue with the criminal proceedings," and as of that date he takes on the role of the prosecutor. According to the law, the role of such a party is called "the injured party as a prosecutor."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This procedure also unfolds before the military court or it's also applicable in military courts.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. There is absolutely no difference. The procedure before a military and civilian court is exactly the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as you know, as far as you can remember, do you remember any cases in which the victims themselves requested that investigations be conducted although the prosecutor had shelved the case? Were there any such cases?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were such cases. Now that you have asked me this question, I can remember one case, a case of murder. The prosecutor established that it was a matter of legitimate defence and that there were no grounds to continue with proceedings. The brother of the victim did not agree with the prosecutor. He filed a request for an investigation, and in fact the accused, Senad Agatovic, who died -- was killed in a traffic accident, later was detained on the basis of this request. Afterwards, I -- I was the presiding judge, and the chamber finally established that it was a matter of legitimate defence. The person was released. That was one such case. There were a number of such cases, not that many, but there were a number of such cases and there are still cases of that kind that are being dealt with. And I, as a lawyer, am now defending someone in one such case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for this technical information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Good morning, witness. I would like to ask you a few questions about a matter you discussed yesterday with us, and that is the matter of the abandoned houses and thefts in abandoned houses. But before I come to my questions, I have still other questions on your time as a judge. I understood yesterday that you became a judge in October 1992, but I don't recall that you have told us when you stopped being a judge in the military court. Could you inform me about the end of your tenure as a military judge.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I started working as a judge on the 12th of October, 1992, and I was a judge in the military court while military courts were in existence. And if I remember this correctly, it was up until 1996. I think it was up until 1996. Then all of us who were judges in the military court, in accordance with the law, became lords of the high court in Zenica, and after the judiciary had been reformed, we competed to become judges of the cantonal court in the 1990s, and that's why I completed my career as a judge in January 2004.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You also told us this morning that you have been a duty judge, apart from being a judge at -- a presiding judge at trials or other judge during trials. Have you also been a -- an investigating judge proper in this period of time, these four years? And if so, when?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was an investigative judge too, since there were a lot of cases and they couldn't be dealt with by one investigative judge, as a result the presiding judge would also appoint someone else if this was possible, and that was my case. But given the total number of cases that I dealt with, I was involved in about 200 investigative cases. That's 200 out of -- whereas, in the case of other cases there was 750.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... judge?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Throughout that period, well, sporadically, temporarily. And when I acted as the duty judge and a request had been filed to conduct investigations by the prosecutor, then I would sometimes continue to work on such cases until the investigation was completed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Thank you. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Judge Swart's question has not been included in the transcript. It was a question of interpretation, I think. I don't know if we could correct this or whether it could be done later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: Yes, it's line 14 on page 45.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... have you been an investigating judge? I'm afraid I made the same mistake now. So I'll try again. My question was: Have you been an investigating judge also? And if so, when? Well, let's continue. Yesterday, witness, you told us about abandoned houses and thefts from abandoned houses, and I made a note of the transcript yesterday of page 59, and I noted the following, and I quote you: "With regard to thefts from these houses, you said the following: "I was thinking whether I could recognise certain intention to perpetrate war crimes or was it just the case of somebody needing a cow, and the easiest thing for him -- for this perpetrator to do was to go to an abandoned house and steal a cow from such an abandoned house." This you said in response to a question of whether such a theft from an abandoned house could amount to a war crime. Now, I've been looking at your statement, and I gather - but please correct me if I'm wrong - that for you to make the distinction is primarily a matter of motive, what is the motive of the perpetrator -- depending on the motive of the perpetrator, something can be a war crime or not be a war crime. Is that a correct impression of what you said? Is that a correct interpretation of what you said?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I regret that you haven't understood me correctly. I wasn't mentioning motives, but as a lawyer I was speaking about the relation of the perpetrator to the consequences of the act. And according to our terminology, this relates to intentions, to intend to -- so the awareness of the perpetrator that by taking certain action this action would have certain legal consequences. And what I wanted to say was that in such cases we did not recognise the intent of the perpetrator to commit a crime but, rather, the intent of the perpetrator to gain property. We took advantage of the fact that property in certain areas had been abandoned and this enabled the perpetrator to obtain quite easily this property. We neglected all other issues of theoretical and legal kind, issues that have to do with civilian law. For example, whether property that's abandoned can be taken. Is this a matter of taking property of -- in certain circumstances? Can this act be considered to be a crime? But since the civilian authorities established orders in order to protect civilian property and it was stated that all abandoned property would be under the control of the state organs, as a result we drew the conclusion that this property hadn't been abandoned in terms of civilian law, and we drew our legal decisions on that basis. We determined that a crime of stealing other people's property had been committed and we would put such perpetrators on trial as a result.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Perhaps I should not have used the word "motive," because that may have a very specific meaning, but I should perhaps have used the word "intent." But then intent is the distinctive criterion for you, or is it not?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. With your leave, the system of describing a crime in the law which is applicable and on the whole is continental is also -- this system is based on the idea of intent, so we say that certain acts can only be committed if there is intent. And there's entire intent or acceptance of the consequences. Certain acts aren't punishable if this intent isn't established. You can't accidentally commit an offence. This was a very important criteria, and we spent a lot of time on trying to establish whether intent was present, because I do agree that any act against property, physical integrity, against other sexes, against personal dignity, et cetera, in the course of wartime could also be described as a war crime against the civilian population. But our position was the following: We discussed this matter, and if there was an isolated event - and we're talking about a collection of isolated events - then the accumulation of such events does not allow one to describe these events as a war crime committed against the civilian population.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're trying to see what you are trying to tell us because yesterday you said that it was the court's responsibility to provide a legal description of the events. Should one draw the following conclusion: That if property was misappropriated and the civilian authorities said that such property should be protected, in your opinion was this worse for the perpetrator of the crime or was it better? What would the consequence be? Stealing something from private property protected by the civilian authorities, is such an act more serious than if something had been stolen and no decisions had been taken by the civilian authorities? Do you understand the question that I am putting to you?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: My answer would be as follows: A crime of aggravated theft in a qualified form which reads "appropriation of abandoned property or elements of property" is the legal description of a criminal offence that we did inherit from the former SFRY. So the amendments made to the Criminal Code changed the law and provided a new criminal offence with a much graver penalty than envisaged for qualified forms in the past, and as soon as we find that abandoned property had been appropriated, this was considered a new objective form for incrimination, and the perpetrator was tried under that stricter provision of the law envisaging a higher penalty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And this is the result of the amendment to the law made in this area. You explained that the former offence in ex-Yugoslavia was modified and that your country envisaged an offence which is sanctioned much more strictly than in the former system.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In that period of time, all the penalties because of a state of war, this was provision of law, of the Rule 226 of the Criminal Code, and it was said the penalty is one to five years. If the act is committed in a condition of immediate threat of war or a state of war, the maximum penalty is ten years. But the bodies responsible for -- to legislate introduced new offences, criminal offences, new one, original ones, for which the penalties were much higher than envisaged for the basic offences. So we had the criminal offence of murder on an ethnic basis or rape on an ethnic basis. Within the framework of property offences, we had this criminal offence of appropriation of abandoned property. You know that the parliament was not functioning during the war. It could not sit. The Presidency of the State had the constitutional right to pass decrees with the force of law whereby laws were amended, and these are the decrees I'm referring to. And as soon as the conditions set in for the parliament to meet, laws were passed to transfer these decrees into law. Some were annulled once the state of war was overcome, so there was no need for them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: So if we read in Article 148 of the -- what I hope is the Criminal Code of Bosnia at the time saying that aggravated theft is punishable by imprisonment for a term of more than one year but not exceeding ten years, then that is not the whole picture? There's also Article 226 of the same Code, saying that in time of war, in time of imminent danger, the penalties are different. Could you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I can confirm is that you are reading the basic text of the law. And if it says in the law that punishment must be at least one year, then the general maximum is 15 years and not 10. And this Article 148 in paragraph 3 was amended by decree and certain corrections were made. Furthermore, there's a decree on amendments to the Criminal Code where all the penalties prescribed by the original provision of Article 184 have been increased. So the minimum penalty was three years of imprisonment, and in some cases even the possibility of a death penalty being passed down was envisaged. I think in October or November 1993 quite a lengthy decree was passed with significant corrections being made, especially with respect to the penalties prescribed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: I accept your explanation, witness. Maybe we don't have the full picture of the legislation in the -- in Bosnia at the time. That is quite possible. But to come back on the issue of the distinction between a war crime and a common theft, so to speak, you said a few minutes ago if it is an isolated offence or a series of isolated offences, then this would not be a war crime. My question to you is the following: Could you define in a more positive way what constitutes a war crime for you? What is the threshold for a theft or a series of thefts becoming a war crime?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think we have to cross the quantitative threshold and one also has to cross the threshold of intent. If a whole area has been abandoned, a whole region, and if in that region cattle is roaming freely, and if you have a situation in which entire villages have been destroyed and there are no roofs on the houses and, on the other hand, you see a neighbouring village has been abandoned with roofs on their houses, what would happen in practice would be that people would go to the abandoned house and take off the tiles to cover their own roofs with. And this was prosecuted and tried as a crime. But in our understanding, it did not acquire the characteristics of a war crime because the perpetrator never had it in his mind to commit a war crime. He knew he was taking somebody else's property. He had motives which from his standpoint were understandable, but according to the legal system we were bound by could only be considered as mitigating circumstances when handing down sentence. So there were a number of circumstances which led us to believe that we were not confronted with organised war crimes, that there is no link between individual perpetrators of this specific criminal offence which could describe their joint efforts as an organised war crime, and we felt that under the circumstances in which we were living it was quite appropriate to sanction such behaviour as a general crime which increased under wartime conditions and which upon the cessation of the war calmed down and was reduced to the customary peacetime average. Furthermore, the way in which those criminal offences were committed, though before the war of course you didn't have abandoned property -- but in the way they were committed, the quantity of criminal elements, the degree of responsibility, did not differ in any way from similar criminal offences committed before the war and even today. In Bosnia-Herzegovina today, we have an increase of sexual offences in relation to wartime. There's an increase of criminal offences in unauthorised production and trafficking of drugs. So we do have a considerable increase of property crime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Would you then give me an example of what would constitute theft in the form of a war crime?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would consider theft to represent a war crime -- let me first go back to the beginning. It is very hard to imagine theft as a war crime. You go and steal somebody's property and to describe that as "war crime," I can hardly imagine it. But I can imagine the following situation being a war crime. For instance, a group of people who by definition would belong to one ethnic group go to a settlement inhabited by members of another ethnic group with the intention of seizing their property because they belong to another ethnic group with the use of weapons, mistreatment, et cetera. That, in my view, would have the characteristics of a war crime. But I must say that the area in which I lived, I never came across any such event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: To pursue your -- your answer, would the fact that a group of persons in an organised way took property from abandoned houses bring this event in -- in the sphere, in the ambit of war crimes?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to try and adjust to your own way of thought. I don't quite understand what you mean when you say "an organised group working in an organised manner." If you are referring to the group that I mentioned in my previous answer, then we could agree that this was a war crime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Let's be specific, then. Let's suppose there is a region abandoned by its inhabitants, some villagers, and let's suppose there's a group of 20 people who -- who work together in getting the -- the furniture, other things of value in these houses and transport them to elsewhere. So the act in cooperation with this other in a systematic way. My question is: When would this constitute a war crime? When not? In your opinion. I'm interested in your opinion.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it is very hard to set the line, the threshold. I think we would have to go further. If this were to be a group, an organised group doing what you just said, if they were doing it systematically, if they were systematically collecting everything from a particular village, then that would most probably be a war crime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Thank you. The -- the Criminal Code, Chapter 16 of the former Yugoslavia code on war crimes has an Article 142, and it speaks about stealing on a large scale of property in my English translation. Is that also an element for you, the large-scale nature of these -- these events, of these thefts? Is that a -- something you would take into account also yourself?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think in your previous question that is precisely what we were discussing. You said that an organised group of 20 men observed in a region to collect all valuables, furniture, et cetera. So that's the kind of criteria we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Would it also matter to you -- I'm exploring your -- your thoughts and trying to get a clear view of the practice in 1993. Would it also matter in your appreciation of the events whether this large-scale thing happened immediately after the -- the village was abandoned or, let's say, 10 or 20 days after? Is that a relevant distinction for you?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to go back for a moment to what I was saying about procedure. A court trying a case is limited by the factual contents in the indictment provided by the prosecutor. In answering one of the questions, I said that the court was bound by facts but not also by the proposed legal qualification of the act. Therefore, if the court found that the acts contained in the indictment did not occur, he could release Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the accused and he could not charge him with some other criminal offence. That is prohibition of a reform of the charge which was applied by us in this way. So if you're asking me as a matter of principle if I had before me these facts that you have referred to, then I would certainly judge differently each situation; that is, my judgement would be different if somebody appropriated and looted a village while resorting to force, then this would be an act which could be qualified as a war crime. But as your question ended with concrete reference to the practice in 1993 and after that, I have to tell you that the court and courts I worked in, with the exception of a couple of cases, did not receive indictments for war crimes in the legal or factual sense, so they couldn't judge them as such. During the war, I did preside over a trial chamber that passed down sentence of death penalty in one case, but there were no charges factually which would allow the court to recognise those offences as war crimes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Well, you have already anticipated some of my next questions, and this is what I wanted to discuss with you too, about a situation. You have been a trial judge, you told us, and you have also been a -- an investigating judge. Well, let's first take the situation of the investigating judge. I come back to what you said yesterday, and a few minutes ago you said the same thing, I suppose. You said yesterday the starting point for determining the nature of an offence are the facts as described by the police or by the public prosecutor. And you also said the following: You could not conclude the possibility of a war crime from these descriptions. And you said something similar a few seconds ago, I believe. Now, you have been an investigating judge too, and you have, I suppose, had cases from the prosecutor in which he invited you to investigate a theft from abandoned houses. Have you had such cases also in your experience?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did have such cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Were there in these cases that you got from the prosecutor to investigate as an investigating judge cases in which you -- you had a feeling this might amount to something more than a common theft, or did you never see such cases?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally did not have such a case, but I have to say on the assumption that I did, I am bound in my investigations as an investigating judge by the facts shown me by the prosecutor in the request for investigation. I investigate what he says in the disposition of his request. He can give a reasonable explanation that someone was raped and say in his proposal of an offence that it is a parking offence. I am, of course, caricaturing things. But by the way the act took place is what limits me in my investigations. I investigate only the facts that are forwarded to the investigating judge by the prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: So to pursue your example further, if the prosecutor would ask you to investigate a parking offence and in the course of your investigation you become aware that a rape has been committed, you must ignore the rape then?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That means that I must complete the investigation into the circumstances requested by the prosecutor, and I would give him all the documents that I have collected in my investigation which he misqualified as a parking offence. Then he can file a request for an extension of the investigation or for an investigation to go into another direction. I am afraid that there may be some misunderstanding. My prosecutor described a rape and I am investigating the rape, but he misqualified it, calling it a parking offence. What he receives in the form of investigation documents, new information, is for the prosecutor for a broader proceeding, but the investigating judge cannot extend the investigation beyond the facts referred to by the prosecutor in his request for an investigation. Even the court in passing judgement cannot overstep the limit and find someone guilty of a more serious crime if that entailed that the description of the crime has to be different from the one contained in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: I understand that as a trial judge you are bound by the indictments and you cannot convict a person for a more serious offence than the offence with which the accused has been charged with. That is a basic principle of criminal procedure in many countries, not only in Bosnia but also in many European countries, for instance. But I am asking you about your position as a investigating judge. You gave an example of a rape and a traffic offence, but I want to go back to the -- the theft of property from abandoned houses. What a war crime and a common crime have in common in this situation is that it is both -- both are offences consisting of taking someone's property without his consent. So my question is: If you are at the request of the prosecutor investigating something that may at any rate be qualified a theft, what is your liberty as an investigating judge to enquire into all the relevant circumstances which would enable the prosecutor to qualify this theft as a war crime or as a common crime? That is really my question.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, that is the whole point over which we don't understand one another. In the legal system that we worked within, an investigation and as a result the role of the investigating judge can be reduced to the following. It says: "I propose an investigation against XY because of well-founded grounds to suspect that on the 1st of September, 1993 at such-and-such an hour, at such-and-such a place he went to an abandoned house of an unknown citizen, a Croat, and took from the house a window and took that window to such-and-such a place and sold it to person AB for so much dinars or German marks or whatever, and thereby he committed an aggravated theft under Article 148 and also article of the decree," and now I am the investigating judge who has received such a request, and attached to that request is the criminal report, two informative statements by witnesses, a receipt on temporary seizure of objects by the military police who caught him red-handed, a receipt that the window or money had been taken from him, et cetera. And I issue a decision and say: "On the basis of the attachments to the request for an investigation, it is my judgement that there are grounds to believe that XY did commit a criminal offence for which the investigation is requested and an investigation will be carried out." In the investigation, in order to confirm the facts indicated by the prosecutor, I will carry out the following steps. So I will interview two witnesses, whose informative statements were attached, and thereby legalise their statements and transform them into evidence, valid evidence during the proceedings. Then I will hear the citizen to whom the object was sold, and I will limit my activities to these boundaries. If when I interview the person to whom the stolen window was sold I learn that this is the tenth stolen window being sold to him by the same person, I will point that out in my note on the interview. And when I proclaim the investigation complete, I will send all this to the prosecutor. The prosecutor will determine on the basis of all of this information whether an additional investigation is required, and he will address the investigating judge and say, "Extend your investigation and find out more about those other nine windows and find witnesses to confirm this." And his decision will be bound by these reports. He cannot, however, issue an indictment for a criminal offence that he did not investigate. And then, of course, the court cannot try a person for a crime he has not been charged with. We never had an investigating judge who would be told the general context along the lines, "Gentlemen, look into what happened in village A." No, he always had to receive very specific information, and any action beyond that would actually be illegal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: So may I conclude from what you said that not only at the trial but also during preliminary investigations the prosecutor determined the scope of the investigation, and if he asks you to investigate an event and he presented that as an isolated theft, then you would have to remain within the limits set by him? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: So that's what I wanted to know, your relationship in the pre-trial stage in this field with the prosecutor. I have some final questions on numbers. You said yesterday, "I sat on 750 cases and I was involved in some 250 proceedings." I had a question there. Were these all cases on -- on theft in abandoned houses, or was this the total of the cases you have dealt with in your period as a judge?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the total number of cases I was involved in while I was a judge at the military court. And, Your Honour, they varied from crimes that we called "forest crimes," and included rape, murder, war crimes, et cetera, because I have said that I even signed a death sentence in the course of my career at the military court. Since we were competent for all crimes committed by members of the military, in those 750 cases I acted as an individual judge and as the presiding judge - we called this "the small chamber" because there was one professional judge and two jurors and there was a larger chamber with two judges and three jurors - so I was -- I investigated about 250 investigations. And on 259 times I went to carry out on-site investigations during those periods.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: You were involved, we heard yesterday, in criminal investigations with respect to theft from abandoned houses, and we have also seen documents in which you play a role as a judge in these kind of offences. My question is: Is it possible for you still after ten years to -- to tell us how many cases of such offences you have seen in your practice? I mean the thefts from -- from houses that were left alone by their inhabitants.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know the statistics. But perhaps one-quarter, perhaps that involved one-quarter of all the cases dealt with. This is just a guess, but I would say that it was about one-quarter of the cases. Usually crimes against property, but naturally these crimes were not crimes committed against property and abandoned houses always. But it was very important for me -- there's something I must add, with your leave -- it was very important for me not only from a legal perspective but also from a moral perspective, as a human being, you know, given such a senseless war that had broken out in my country. There were a lot of issues that were matters of priority. I don't want to be pathetic, but we were hungry, we had no electricity, no water. We didn't have the basic medical supplies that were required, and the military and civilian authorities had to face senseless aggression, forces that wanted to destroy everything that was human and positive. And given such conditions, one could find the force and the resources to punish individuals who had stolen a couple of items, a couple of chairs that had been thrown out into the yard of an abandoned house. I thought this was important to -- I thought it was important for us to be able to do this in the circumstances. I thought it was important to have the moral force to deal with such problems, and I didn't believe that -- that we were not acting professionally. I believe that we were able to operate in a very functional and correct manner, and this is still my belief today, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: I fully understand the feelings that you must have had in investigating or trying these cases, but I am only looking for a quantitative indication of the phenomenon in your work. I guess from your answer you may conclude that some -- one-quarter of your cases were property crimes and that you were -- it is difficult for you to further specify the number of -- the percentage of crimes consisting of thefts in abandoned houses? Is that a correct interpretation?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you are quite right. I really couldn't specify that number today. I expected you to ask me that question, and I'm trying to think back to these events.
