But I believe that there were after all more cases of general theft than of cases of theft of items from abandoned houses, and for a very simple reason: In the territory over which my court had jurisdiction, there were abandoned houses, but fortunately the population wasn't being systematically persecuted. As a result, the property hadn't been widely dispersed throughout the area, and that was the case in certain other areas, where you had areas that were completely empty and no one had remained there. You know, the authorities in the area where I lived made efforts to protect people and their property, and that was not the case for other authorities who acted in a contrary manner. So the abandoned property that could have been plundered -- well, there wasn't so much property. This is my interpretation, and I can't provide you with any periods, but if I go back to the period, I believe that the number of such cases was not as great as the number of other crimes. And naturally, given the nature of this case, I believe that the chamber, given evidence that was being presented to it, might arrive at an erroneous conclusion. Because if you have a look at what's been placed on the table here, then all we can see such cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Again, I understand that this is a difficult question to answer. You talked about your area in your answer. When you talk about your area, do you mean the -- the district of the -- the area over which the Zenica military court was -- had jurisdiction, or is it a more loosely way of using the word "area" in your answer?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I said "area," Your Honour, I was referring to any area which was under the control of the legal authorities of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and that in military terms was under the control of the ABiH. It happened that I had the opportunity of seeing that the situation in many other areas was identical, because given the role I had and the duties I had to perform and given the decree law issued to military courts which states that if one military court cannot operate in its own territory, it will be replaced by the closest military court. So as a result, I was also involved in the area of Sarajevo as a deputy judge. So when I am referring to these matters, I'm referring to the entire area, but in particular to the area over which the district military court had jurisdiction, and this overlaps with the territory under the control of the 3rd Corps of the ABiH, at least to a very large extent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Thank you. I still had a more difficult question in mind for you, and that was the question whether you could specify how many cases of abandoned houses and thefts from abandoned houses you dealt with in 1993, but I understand that this would really be an answer that you cannot -- really be a question that you could not possibly answer at Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. this moment, so I will not put that question to you. Thank you very much for your answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I'll now give the floor to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Only briefly, before I try to come back to the numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: One issue: You told us -- or you told to His Honour Judge Swart that it was important for you to do that, I guess, to -- to investigate these things. And I quote you that you said that there was a "moral force to deal with these problems." Do you mean, you know, to -- despite the times of war, to deal with these criminal offences; that was important for you?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In spite of the fact that war was raging, Mr. Prosecutor, it was very important for me to be able to deal with criminal cases -- or rather, those whose duty it was to carry out actions that would lead to instituting criminal proceedings, I was glad that we had enough force to deal with criminal cases and to investigate such cases. You've reduced what I said to a personal opinion, you know. That's my belief. I am a Bosnian, and I am a patriot, and when the war broke out I was 39 years old. I was fit for military service and had I received call-up papers, I would have immediately responded. That's what I wanted to say. It was very important for me to live in an area that hadn't been engulfed by hatred, that hadn't been engulfed by immorality. I was living in circumstances that could be qualified as historically responsible, and it was very important for me to be able to live with people. The fact that I was living with people there was very important. And generally speaking, they were victims as a people. Marko Vesevic, the poet, who is a member of my ethnic community, the Serbian community said on one occasion, "Gentlemen, what is happening is Bosnia is not a war. It is the elimination of the Muslims. It's killing Muslims." It was very important for me in the area where I was born and in which there were far fewer Muslims than in 1992 -- it was important for me that there was a system there in which we tried to respect the law. And I believe that all those who had been identified as perpetrators of a crime should be reported and processed and sentenced. This was done -- this is very important. It was important for this to be done on the basis of evidence. No one was sentenced without evidence -- no one was convicted without any evidence, nor was anyone accused of having committed a certain crime because his name was of a certain kind and spoke one of the three languages that you refer to with an abbreviation that consists of three letters. That's what I wanted to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And if nobody had acted like you and your colleagues and the authorities, had looked into these cases, had investigated them, prosecuted them, what would have been the message to the people on the ground if these crimes would have went unpunished, uninvestigated?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: What would the message have been? The message would have been that they should first flee from the area and then that they should never return there and everything would have been senseless. We would have all been the same. In Zenica, the situation would have been identical to the situation in, let's say, Prijedor, and the situation we had there was such that anyone who did not want to leave did not have to leave. And believe me, not thanks to me but thanks to General Hadzihasanovic, because the people who were involved in the combat at the time, they had, as we say, both a loaf of bread and a knife in their hands. But the composition of the -- or the military police and the civilian police weren't fully dedicated to their work -- or if --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: If they hadn't been fully dedicated to their work, then the military court would have just been "trompe l'oeil," and I wouldn't have had anything to do. I wouldn't have had any work to do. The military court would have existed just for show.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And you would agree with me that if alleged perpetrators aren't looked after, that would leave a sense of impunity which would encourage others to follow and commit crimes? Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I fully agree with that. But I'm just wondering whether you're going to continue to ask me the same question by rephrasing it a number of times. Let's deal with this once and for all. I fully agree with you that any event that is qualified as a crime should be investigated. Its perpetrator should be identified and punished. This is called "general prevention in peacetime," and it's part of -- of the law in all countries throughout the world. This naturally does not mean that it's possible to identify each and every perpetrator. This isn't possible in beautiful Holland or in Switzerland and even less in Bosnia, where there was a war raging. But if you seriously examine the statistics, I believe that you will see that the percentage of perpetrators identified in Bosnia and Herzegovina - and I'm referring to the area I lived in - that percentage in comparison to the number of people, or reported the number of cases of criminal reports, is greater than in Germany in the year 2004.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And the principle of general prevention not only applies in peacetime but perhaps even more in -- in times of war.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Naturally. It's important. General prevention is always important. That's why according to the law in certain situations you have to publish court decisions in the media. But naturally. Thank God that that's the situation in the war. General prevention in wartime doesn't only have an effect on potential perpetrators of crimes. It has a significance that's quite different. It also sends a message to potential victims. The message that if certain situations arise, they'll be protected, and these potential victims can then take decisions as to how they want to organise their lives. You know, you're -- if you had asked me this question, it would have been impolite, but I'll answer this question that you haven't put to me. In 1992 and 1993, I was a Serb and I had all the characteristics that this denotes. My assessment wasn't based on patriotism alone. I'm too old and too well-educated. I've travelled a lot, so I wouldn't take any decisions without such criteria. On the basis of those criteria, I decided that my family and I should remain in the area where -- where we were when the war broke out, and believe me, I didn't make a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let me just briefly return to the issue of -- of numbers. And perhaps you can -- you can answer it; perhaps not. Do you recall of all the cases you were involved - the same time frame Judge Swart referred to - how many were purely military offences, meaning desertion or disobeying orders, abandoning front lines, as opposed to, you know, the -- the theft of property of abandoned houses? How many were purely typical military offences in percentage, if you can tell us?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the percentage. But if you ask me -- well, I arrived there in October 1992. At the time, we had quite a lot of cases, a lot of cases that involved service in an enemy force. The number of these cases was then reduced and many of those cases were then -- were described as illegal possession of arms and explosives. They were given a less serious crime. And I know that up until the end of 1992 and at the beginning of 1993 this was the situation. Afterwards, there were certain events in the territory of the district military court in Sarajevo. It had to do with certain -- with certain events in the ranks of the ABiH. The command believed that there had been an armed rebellion in the Juka Prazina Special Unit. I then went to Igman because the Sarajevo judges weren't able to do so given the encirclement of Sarajevo; they could not leave the town. And two or three months later we were involved in this purely military matter. Then I know that we worked intensively on two types of crimes: One was -- the first was the crime of refusing to accept the call-up papers, of avoiding one's military service; and there were also the crimes of willfully abandoning the armed forces. This concerned a period during which the troops were being disciplined. This is an important period and it coincides with the time when the 3rd Corps was being established. And many events of willful abandonment were processed, many cases of selling weapons. There was also the crime of inappropriate treatment of weapons issued, cases of refusing to obey orders, cases of abuse in the course of military service. Certain military policemen had been reported. Also in the battalion within the corps. So when the court was established, the court received a lot of criminal reports that came under this heading, "Criminal reports against the armed forces." We had one or two cases that involved betrayal, abandoning military equipment. So those were cases under that heading. And the majority of cases at that period of time were of such a nature. Later I remember something else. At the beginning of 1994, the -- there was a rise in the rate of murder and we had to deal with this. This is no longer of interest to this case here, but -- and later -- again, this is not something that interests you, but there were cases of people who appropriated property that had been given them to guard temporarily. And this was then punished. But I think that in 1993, in the spring of 1993 and afterwards, most of the cases -- most of the criminal cases were of this kind. And we knew that this corps was being established, we knew that there were large-scale changes being introduced there, and I know that they even said that a scarecrow had arrived in the 3rd Corps, and they were referring to General Hadzihasanovic, and that everything would be strict and hard as of that -- from that time onwards. These are statistics that can be found very easily. All the archives are still in existence. All the records are still in existence. And it's easy to see how the cases arrived at the court, how we dealt with them, and how we processed them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And my last question is, again, about these numbers, and hopefully it can be a little bit shorter. How many cases involved the members of the armed forces or the -- the warring parties, like HVO perpetrators against ABiH victims and the other way around? Have you dealt with any such cases at all? And if so, in your opinion, recollection, how many cases involved perpetrators, HVO or ABiH on the one side against the victims or the other warring party on the other side, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that there were any such cases that I was involved in. A moment ago a case that you mentioned had to do with the killing by the HVO of two civilians on a public road. The HVO after the division did not recognise our jurisdiction. They set up their own judicial system. Just as they formed their own state, they had their own prosecutor, their own courts. So I do not recollect any case with such characteristics that you have referred to.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. It is 25 to 1.00. We shall have the break, and we will resume at 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I shall now give the floor to the Defence for any additional questions they may have.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Veseljak, let us continue with the set of questions relating to numbers, as my learned friend said. You said yourself that during the war you tried more than 700 cases and participated in about 200 investigations. Before that, you said that during the war there were a total of eight criminal judges in the court.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: On average, eight. Sometimes one less or one more.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: If we wanted to find out the total number of cases processed, would that mean that the numbers you gave should be multiplied by the number of colleagues you had in court or do you believe that your colleagues didn't have as many?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I worked on slightly more cases, so I don't think you could multiply it with eight, but roughly. I did -- I was involved in a slightly larger number of cases than others.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In any event, during the war, it would amount to several thousand cases.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, the persons against which you conducted trials, who were those persons? Were they civilians or military?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In an enormous majority of cases, they were military personnel.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Earlier you told us about the duties of the military police and the civilian police who filed criminal reports. Tell me, to what extent and in what percentage of cases in the phase of filing criminal reports when the prosecutor is given the possibility of starting proceedings, did the 3rd Corps participate, its military police battalion, and other brigades and battalions? Were they in most cases the bodies filing criminal reports which were tried by your court?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The percentage of criminal reports submitted by others as compared to the number of criminal reports filed by the 3rd Corps or, rather, the military police battalion was negligible.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: This fact that you just testified to that most of those proceedings were instituted on the basis of criminal reports filed by the 3rd Corps and its military police battalion and other units, is it linked in any way to your testimony that the army endeavoured to prevent and investigate every crime? Is this linked?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, please. There's on objection by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, thanks. Also, the previous question, were most of these cases 3rd Corps, that's a leading question. All these words are indicative of an answer. And I also wonder whether that really arises of the issues which the Judges concerned. I don't think there was any mentioning of the 3rd Corps military police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The Defence, could you rephrase your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that my questions were Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. related to questions of my colleague, who spoke of the military police, and the Judges, who referred to military units.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said that all organs under control of the army and the legal authorities sought to create an environment of security. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, how do you assess such a large number of criminal reports filed by the army or its security organs?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: My assessment is that this was a clear example of respect of the law by the army and its organs.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: My learned friend asked you about criminal offences linked to purely military discipline. My question is: To what extent disciplining the army or prosecuting the military for acts linked to military orders, failure to obey, abandoning the front, et cetera, to what extent efforts to discipline the army are linked to crime prevention, prevention of crimes being committed by the same army.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are directly linked and very important. I have to remind you that we were living under circumstances when there was a decision on a general public mobilisation, which theoretically meant that we were all part of the army. If you managed to discipline the largest entity in the population, you're really establishing public discipline throughout because people would reason as follows: If the army prosecutes its own members, then obviously the army is endeavouring to establish the rule of law and peace, law and order.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You also said that there were undiscovered criminal offences. My question is whether in that period of time there were certain factors which had a decisive impact on the ability to discover each and every perpetrator.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the second part of your question, you corrected the first part of that question, which was not precise. We can't speak about -- about undiscovered criminal offences but unidentified perpetrators. And there were a series of factors which were an obstacle to detecting every perpetrator. I referred to some of them yesterday, and I am going to repeat today. People without ID documents, a territory segmented and fragmented, certain arrangements of a territorial and political nature which were contrary to the Constitution, a significant fluctuation of the population, the killing of perpetrators of criminal offences. We would frequently discover that the perpetrator of an offence subsequently was killed. Then also the deaths of witnesses who got killed either as civilians or as members of this or that army, obstacles in the form of logistics, the shortage of certain resources, the lack of freedom of movement, inability to access the scene of crimes, the moving-out of perpetrators that we suspected to an area which came under a different jurisdiction, and so on. There were many reasons that hampered and often prevented this.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: My learned friend also asked you in connection with various types of criminal offences. My question is: Did you process and try the -- for perpetrators of criminal offences of impermissible trafficking and trade?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did have the following situation: This is a picture that I don't think people will be able to understand who didn't experience what we did. There was something that we called a flea market. There was a shortage of everything, and on that market sometimes stolen goods would appear. And military police patrols would tour these flea markets and take in persons selling goods at such places, and they were processed for the criminal offence of unlawful trade. And if you catch somebody selling a stolen telephone, then in his defence he would tell you how he got hold of that telephone, and then in that way we would discover the thief, the person who stole that good. So we had many cases of unlawful trade.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In answer to a question of His Honour the Judge, you answered questions about the position of the damaged party if the prosecutor doesn't institute proceedings. Tell me, please: If the prosecutor has material that does not point to a particular perpetrator, known or unknown; for instance, if he only has his on-site investigation report and the assessment that there's no reason to suspect that a criminal offence had been committed, is he then in a position to reject that material or those documents or to shelve those documents? Is the position of the damaged party different -- does it slightly differ from what you explained to Their Honours?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe we didn't quite understand one another. In the situation when on the basis of facts or information collected the prosecutor comes to the conclusion that the acts presented do not constitute a criminal offence and he decides to suspend the investigation, he will inform the damaged party that within a period of eight days he can continue the prosecution. If the prosecutor doesn't find a single piece of evidence that an act took place, then logically the damaged party does not exist, so he has no one to inform.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: That is precisely what I wanted to see, whether there's any difference between a prosecutor making a decision and him failing to inform someone. You have explained that now. In view of the wartime conditions under which the prosecutor was working, as were all the other bodies, tell me to what extent those circumstances contributed to lack of knowledge about the injured party, who he was, where he was, or was he always accessible to the judiciary?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that I can say that very frequently the injured party was not accessible and he was not even known. The police found a man who was carrying an object, established that he had stolen it somewhere. You can't find out who it belongs to or under which circumstances he stole it. You yourself showed a number of documents speaking about the processing of the stealing of the property of an unknown owner, and you can't inform such an unknown owner about the investigation.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: His Honour Judge Swart asked you several questions in relation to abandoned houses, and explaining the procedure you mentioned what the investigating judge is bound by when a request is addressed to him by the prosecutor. You gave an example that in the description a rape was described; whereas, the investigating judge qualified it as a parking offence for the sake of argument. Tell me, as an investigating judge, were you bound by that legal qualification given by the prosecutor during the investigation stage already now?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The investigating judge was not bound except to the following extent: There was a situation in which the investigating judge would assess that the quantity of information regarding suspicion does not in the least lead to a criminal offence being committed. So there is a situation when the investigating judge is -- opposes an investigation, and if an investigating judge expresses this disagreement in an official note, then the final decision would be made by the court -- by the trial chamber consisting of three professional judges, and that would be the final decision. So only if the investigating judge finds that on the basis of documents provided to him there aren't any elements to support a well-founded suspicion.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please: In other situations, when a decision is taken to carry out an investigation, you as an investigating judge, what would you say in the description of the rape, that such a person on such-and-such a day raped somebody? What would you put down as the crime, regardless of what the investigating judge said?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: We would copy the description from the prosecutor, yet the qualification we would change. A change -- any change in the disposition would be unlawful in both the subjective and objective sense. We were always linked to the individual and to the description.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Explaining to His Honour to what extent you assessed a certain act which you were investigating or trying, you referred to new characteristics of the criminal offence of theft, that is, new sanctions prescribed by the decree with the force of law. Mr. Veseljak, as I have a collection of all the Official Gazettes from 1992, were you referring to the decree with the force of law amending the decree on the implementation of the Criminal Code of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Criminal Code of SFRY taken over as the republican law in conditions of immediate threat of war and state of war, published in Official Gazette no. 21 dated the 23rd of November, 1992 on pages 570, 571, and 572?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But there's another one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, I don't think that's really contested, but it's obviously highly leading. My learned friend is testifying right now.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I believe quite the opposite. The witness mentioned this decree. In his answer he said 1993. And as I have the decree in front of me, I thought it would be a good idea for the witness to confirm whether he referred to this decree, which drastically increased the sanctions for certain criminal offences, and I don't see why this is leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Veseljak, answering a question from His Honour Judge Swart, you said that the minimum penalty was three years up to the death penalty for the criminal offence of theft from abandoned property; is that right? Tell me, please, whether there were any other offences for which much higher sentences were envisaged, including the death penalty, if committed by a military man and if it had to do with abandoned property.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The same offence committed by a civilian was sanctioned more leniently than one committed by a military personnel. The -- the fact that somebody was in the military meant that the stricter law would be implied -- would be applied.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I'm now asking you as a judge: Is this the decree you were referring to and which the judges were obliged to implement?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This can be seen from the documents that were on my table a moment ago which you provided or the Prosecutor in which when giving the legal qualification of an act we referred to the basic text of the law, and I think it is Article 10 of this decree which provides for stricter sanctions, and this can be seen from the judgements, and certainly that was the decree amended the law and it became law and we implemented it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you were speaking about the number of criminal offences and their qualification in answer to His Honour the Judge, you provided some clarification as to kind of -- the descriptions of acts that you received. Tell me, please: When viewing that period, were all the events discovered, processed, as far as you know, regardless of whether that act was qualified in one way or another?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I can answer in the affirmative, that all events were processed with the description given by the prosecutor and his proposal as to the legal qualification to be given.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Since as a judge you were active throughout the war, can you tell us that these thefts, and particularly thefts from abandoned property, did they occur over a short period of time or did you come across such thefts throughout the war?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Throughout the war, for the duration of the war. And I even think, as far as I can now remember -- I don't think one particular period could be identified. Perhaps the majority of thefts occurred during the period of hunger in 1994, which was so drastic that I, as someone receiving a salary, on average would eat once in three days. And I think that the incidents of thefts was higher in that period.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Now that you have referred to this period of hunger, were civilians also hungry and did they steal?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, civilians were hungry too.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know how many civilians were prosecuted in regular courts for similar offences?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN VESELJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the number, but I know that my dear colleagues in basic courts and the higher court competent for aggravated thefts had their hands full at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Since you have already answered some questions I had in mind in answering questions from my learned friend, I have no more questions for you and I thank you for answering them for me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The other Defence team?

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No questions. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, your testimony has been completed. During two days, you answered all the questions put both by the Defence and the Prosecution, as well as the Judges. I wish to thank you for this. And on behalf of the Chamber, we wish you a safe journey home and success in your new professional as an attorney-at-law. And I also wish you all the best in your professional activities. I should like to ask the usher to accompany you out.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I say one sentence before thanking the Court? It was an honour, Mr. President and Your Honours, to testify in this Tribunal. I did not have the possibility of saying something in response to what you said at the beginning, and that is that the Tribunal is not on anyone's side and I have the pressing need to tell you that I was brought here as a witness by the Defence. I, too, am not on anyone's side. And I repeat once again my oath that whatever I told this Court is the truth and nothing but the truth. Thank you very much, and I wish you every success in your activities.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, on page 79, line 12, the answer of the witness does not appear in the transcript. I asked whether civilians stole as well, and the witness said yes, that they too were processed. And line 12 does not reflect that answer of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, we take note of that. We have a quarter of an hour left. We won't have time to bring in the witness, but there is the question of documents. I noted that on the list of documents you indicated that these documents would also be used for another witness. In that case, you will wait for the next witness before requesting admission of those documents into evidence? Are we in agreement?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. As tomorrow we will have the next witness, perhaps it would be best for us to tender the documents after we have heard that witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. As for the Prosecution, there were two documents, number 2 and number 14.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I did not use number 14, so I don't tender it. And Exhibit number 2 has also been the -- the -- or tab number 2 has also been tab number 2 of the first category of the Defence exhibit, on-site investigations. So assuming that the Defence will eventually tender that document - and that's the Zenica 19th April 1993 report - then I don't need to tender anything in this regard. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We will go into private session now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
